newsitem.title: USA: New ISI index to measure U.S. economic strength.
newsitem.headline: New ISI index to measure U.S. economic strength.

text.p: A new weekly index of U.S. business conditions from International Strategy & Investment (ISI) Group Inc provides a coincident indicator of economic strength and an alternative to government reports, ISI said.
Earlier on Monday, ISI reported its Company Survey Index fell to 50.9 in the week ended August 15 from 53.6 the prior week. The four-week moving average rose to 52.1 from 52.0.
"It's a very good coincident indicator of how strong the economy is," said Jason Trennert, a vice president at ISI who manages the survey project.
Investors should monitor the changes in the index from week to week -- particularly in the four-week average -- rather than the overall index level, Trennert said.
The Company Survey Index reflects the sentiment of executives in about 100 firms involved in retail sales, automobile sales, manufacturing, homebuilding and bank loans.
Each week, ISI asks the managers to rate sales on a scale of one (weak) to five (strong). It then tabulates the responses to calculate an index ranging between zero and 100.
ISI has conducted its survey for a few years as part of an effort to keep tabs on the economy, but this week marked the first public release of the index, Trennert said.
"We forecast interest rates and the economy, and we rely on this measure quite a bit in our calculus of how things are," he said.
For each of the past eight weeks, the four-week average has risen, generally in small increments of a tenth or two.
"It basically means that business is running ahead," Trennert said of the survey's performance over the past several weeks. "It's clearly getting stronger."
Trennert said he plans to include other industries in the calculation in the future -- tentatively: technology, trucking, shipping, airlines and commercial construction.
ISI has collected data from these industries already, and while their inclusion probably will alter the index level, it should not have much impact on the week-to-week changes, Trennert said.
Noting longstanding gripes about volatility and inconsistency in official U.S. government economic reports, Trennert said investors appreciate private-sector releases.
"There's been a fairly big distrust of the government numbers. People feel they are either inaccurate, or lacking in some way, or not timely," he said.
ISI, a broker-dealer specializing in economic research, was founded in 1991 by economists Ed Hyman and Nancy Lazar.
